Editor: Piedmont has a history of using city resources to exclude non-white families from the community. But we have an opportunity to redress those wrongs because state law requires California cities to find sites for low-income housing. To avoid again using city power to exclude, segregate, and stigmatize residents, current City of Piedmont policy is to “Support equitable distribution of affordable units across the City.” City staff has unveiled a draft list of sites that mostly complies with the policy of equitable distribution although nearly half of the 211 required low-income units appear in the city corporation yard in Moraga Canyon. City Council reaction to the draft list will, in large part, determine how far Piedmont has come from our exclusionary past. The Council’s most telling choice will be whether to comply with the city’s stated policy of “equitable distribution of affordable units across the city.” Equitable distribution has become an issue because public comment includes the recommendation that the Council reassign low-income units from elsewhere in Piedmont to Blair Park across Moraga Avenue from the 100 units assigned to the corporation yard. Blair Park is an isolated former landfill where pedestrians and bicyclists regularly encounter speeding vehicles with drivers whose sight corridors are limited by the curves of Moraga Avenue. Indeed, pedestrian use of Moraga Avenue proved so dangerous that a plan to locate soccer fields in Blair Park a decade ago had to be abandoned. The Safer Streets Plan recently adopted by OPINIONthe Council states, moreover, that “The Moraga Avenue/Red Rock Road location has been removed from the 2014 list (i.e., of pedestrian safety improvements) because of feasibility issues in providing adequate pedestrian access in Blair Park…” An observer aware of Piedmont’s history and of the suggestion to locate nearly all the 210 State-required low-income units in Blair Park, could reasonably conclude that we had reverted to our exclusionary past. Stigmatizing low-income families by isolating them in Blair Park would reek of a history most Piedmonters regret. I endorse use of the corporation yard for low-income housing. But as a Piedmonter who believes that our shameful history compels us to honor our inclusionary policies, I object to leaving open the possibility of reassigning housing units now shown elsewhere to Blair Park. Such a reassignment would signal a cynical reversion to the despicable exclusionary policies of the last century. The Council should honor current policy and explicitly reject such reassignment. –Ralph Catalano 1139 Oakland Avenue, Piedmont, CA 94611 Phone: 652-2051 • email: news@piedmontpost.org Publisher & Editor: Gray Cathrall City Editor: Allyson Aleksey PRODUCTION MANAGER Victor Cheng REPORTERS Jay Russell Ed Gilligan SCHOOLS Ada Cliff SPORTS Jonathan Comeaux B. articles.text: Piedmont Police Department (PPD) partnered with University of Texas, San Antonio (UTSA) researchers on July 19, 2021 to conduct an analysis of calls for service. The city released the results of the analysis and its key findings on May 20. The city contracted the services of Dr. Michael Smith and Dr. Rob Tillyer from UTSA to analyze five years of data from the PPD. The purpose of the study was to analyze calls for service for frequency of bias-related calls from the public, and use information gathered as a basis for police intervention. The University focused its research on the type of calls for service which officers respond to. The city stated that the work is “part of the effort to understand bias and the historical role racism has played in Piedmont and the community-at-large, in order to better lead a city which is a safe, welcoming, and equitable place for all people committed to by the City Council in Resolution 60-2020.” “A key question that many communities are asking themselves, is whether there are alternatives to police response for certain types of calls,” Dr. Smith said. “What we’re interested in helping the city understand is the impact of calls that come into the department, how [that] drives [the department’s] responses, and whether or not there are potential racial or ethnic disparities in those calls.” The scope of the data covers July 2016 to July 2021, or a fiveyear range of data. The data report states that “[Piedmont] and Police Chief Jeremy Bowers were interested in an analysis that would examine the potential problem of bias by proxy in the city.” Key findings The majority of calls to the department over the five-year period involved ‘checking for evidence of a theft/burglary’ (14.9%), report of a ‘burglar alarm’ (12.7%), responding to ‘suspicious circumstances’ (9.1%), ‘ambulance emergency’ (7.4%), and ‘parking complaints’ (5.5%). The average time it took for an officer to respond to a call was four minutes, and 30% of calls resulted in officer arrival in under one minute. According to the UTSA report, some [focus group] participants expressed concerns about young people from outside the community coming into Piedmont to commit property crimes and were appreciative that PPD is responsive to concerns about suspicious persons when called. Other respondents were “clearly sensitive to being perceived as racially biased,” and expressed that PPD should not respond to calls about suspicious-looking individuals unless callers can specifically describe behaviors or mannerisms that suggest the potential for criminal activity. There was a consensus among the focus group participants about “the need for community engagement and education by the PPD on when residents should call the police about suspicious persons in their neighborhoods, what behaviors to watch out for, and questions to expect from PPD call- takers when residents call to report suspicious behavior.” To view the report in full, visit https://piedmont.ca.gov/government/city_news___notifications/ police_call_data_analysis_town_ hall_meeting_5_23. The published report includes questions asked to focus group participants and more key findings.
articles.title: Police Dept. studies key findings of Univ. of Texas study

articles.text: Piedmont Planning Department is now allowing residents to schedule building permit inspections online rather than come to City Hall. The city rolled out the new feature on May 9 – previously, building inspections had to be made by calling the department directly to book. To schedule a building inspection, visit https://www.piedmont. ca.gov/services___departments/ planning___building/building_ inspections. Select the date of your desired inspection. Appointments can be made 48 hours in advance of the date selected. To schedule an inspection online, you will need the property address, building permit number, your name, phone and email address, and the type of inspection. Daily inspection schedules will be posted on the city’s website by 9 a.m. every day. The city noted that this is an interim improvement that will likely last until the end of 2022, when the city expects to roll our a new public portal designed that residents may use to schedule inspections. Police Dept. studies key findings of Univ. of Texas study By Allyson Aleksey Piedmont Police Department (PPD) partnered with University of Texas, San Antonio (UTSA) researchers on July 19, 2021 to conduct an analysis of calls for service. The city released the results of the analysis and its key findings on May 20. The city contracted the services of Dr. Michael Smith and Dr. Rob Tillyer from UTSA to analyze five years of data from the PPD. The purpose of the study was to analyze calls for service for frequency of bias-related calls from the public, and use information gathered as a basis for police intervention. The University focused its research on the type of calls for service which officers respond to. The city stated that the work is “part of the effort to understand bias and the historical role racism has played in Piedmont and the community-at-large, in order to better lead a city which is a safe, welcoming, and equitable place for all people committed to by the City Council in Resolution 60-2020.” “A key question that many communities are asking themselves, is whether there are alternatives to police response for certain types of calls,” Dr. Smith said. “What we’re interested in helping the city understand is the impact of calls that come into the department, how [that] drives [the department’s] responses, and whether or not there are potential racial or ethnic disparities in those calls.” The scope of the data covers July 2016 to July 2021, or a fiveyear range of data. The data report states that “[Piedmont] and Police Chief Jeremy Bowers were interested in an analysis that would examine the potential problem of bias by proxy in the city.” Key findings The majority of calls to the department over the five-year period involved ‘checking for evidence of a theft/burglary’ (14.9%), report of a ‘burglar alarm’ (12.7%), responding to ‘suspicious circumstances’ (9.1%), ‘ambulance emergency’ (7.4%), and ‘parking complaints’ (5.5%). The average time it took for an officer to respond to a call was four minutes, and 30% of calls resulted in officer arrival in under one minute. According to the UTSA report, some [focus group] participants expressed concerns about young people from outside the community coming into Piedmont to commit property crimes and were appreciative that PPD is responsive to concerns about suspicious persons when called. Other respondents were “clearly sensitive to being perceived as racially biased,” and expressed that PPD should not respond to calls about suspicious-looking individuals unless callers can specifically describe behaviors or mannerisms that suggest the potential for criminal activity. There was a consensus among the focus group participants about “the need for community engagement and education by the PPD on when residents should call the police about suspicious persons in their neighborhoods, what behaviors to watch out for, and questions to expect from PPD call- takers when residents call to report suspicious behavior.” To view the report in full, visit https://piedmont.ca.gov/government/city_news___notifications/ police_call_data_analysis_town_ hall_meeting_5_23. articles.text: City Council approved the appropriation of an additional $30,000 from the facilities maintenance fund to pay for four electric vehicle (EV) charging stations on Magnolia Avenue by the Exedra. The city entered into a 10-year agreement with East Bay Community Energy (EBCE) for the project which initially was promoted as free. “The request for additional funds is related to the inclusion of an American with Disabilities Act (ADA) compliant parking space, and the sidewalk and curb ramp improvements that will be included as a result,” said Gonzales. “This additional component of the project will increase accessibility to Piedmont Park and the EV chargers for all our residents and park users. Unfortunately, EBCE doesn’t have the budget for these ADA improvements and as a result the city will be funding them.” The chargers on Magnolia are designed to provide EV charging service to four parking spaces, including one space to account for Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) requirements. articles.text: Alessandra Lanzara, a Piedmont resident and Physics Professor at the University of California in Berkeley is among the 261 members nominated this year to the American Academy of Art and Science (AAAS). The Academy is widely acknowledged as one of the most prestigious in the world. With this election Lanzara joins the company of illustrious AAAS members spanning multiple fields and professions starting with the founders of the Academy: John Adams, Benjamin Franklin, Alexander Hamilton, and George Washington. Celebrated leaders, artists and scientists that profoundly shaped society have been members since, such as John F. Kennedy, Martin Luther King, Jr., Nelson Mandela, Georgia O’Keeffe, Gabriel Garcia Márquez, Alexander Graham Bell, Charles Darwin and Albert Einstein, in addition to more than 250 Nobel and Pulitzer Prize winners. “We are celebrating a depth of achievements in a breadth of areas,” said David Oxtoby, President of the American Academy. “These individuals excel in ways that excite us and inspire us at a time when recognizing excellence, commending expertise, and working toward the common good is absolutely essential to Alessandra Lanzara (left), children Daniel and Raffaello Banin, and huband Yoav Banin. Alessandra Lanzara in her laboratory at UC Berkeley, where she is an Endowed Professor and the Charles Kittel Chair in Physics. realizing a better future.” The new members will work together with the Academy to set the direction of research and analysis in science and technology policy, global security and international affairs, social policy, education, and the arts and humanities. “It is an incredible honor for me to join a circle of thinkers and visionaries who have inspired the history of humanity. As an immigrant to this country, this recognition means even more to me. Leaving my country and my family has required many sacrifices and to overcome a lot of challenges. Today, being awarded with this incredible recognition makes it all worthwhile,” said Lanzara. Lanzara arrived in the U.S. from Rome, Italy in 1999 to conduct post-doctoral research at Stanford University. “I thought I was going to be here for only six months,” Lanzara said, “but life often has a different plan for us, so here I am 20 years later.” Lanzara joined UC Berkeley’s physics faculty in 2002 and is the founder and director of the Center for Sustainable Materials and Innovation. She works in the area of quantum materials, materials where quantum phenomena dictate exceptional new properties. “If we are able to understand the fundamental physics that drives these properties, then we will be able to harvest these materials to drive revolutionary advances in electronics, quantum computing, energy and medical imaging,” said Lanzara. Lanzara has also been an active advocate for women in science and a promoter of kids engaging with science from a young age. She has served on the Scientific Board of the Lawrence Hall of Science, presented at the Scienza Palooza Fair, spoken at Nano High, and has been on the board of Piedmont Makers. Lanzara resides in Piedmont with her husband, Yoav Banin, an entrepreneur and Chief Product Officer at Nauto, and her two sons, Daniel Banin, a sophomore at Piedmont High School and Raffaello Banin, an 8th grader at Piedmont Middle School. “Piedmont is an incredible community; I have found many friends here and it has been great to see my kids thrive over the years through the Piedmont school system, inspired by incredible and dedicated teachers. I hope I can help to set a strong science program in the high school and continue being an inspiration for young women and young kids who want to pursue a scientific career,” said Lanzara. This article was written by staff members of The Piedmont Highlander, the student newspaper at Piedmont High School. articles.text: There is a common misconception that summer vacation is a relic of the agrarian past when kids would be let out of school in the summer to help with the farming duties. While there is some truth to the notion that kids in rural communities took time off from school to help, this happened in the spring and fall when planting and harvesting occurred. Winter and summer were when many schools in agrarian societies met since that is when the kids had more free time. So where did the summer break come from? Escaping the heat. Before the school calendars were nationally synchronized, many schools were open yearround and students showed up whenever they could or chose to. The extreme heat of the East Coast summers caused many urban residents to escape to cooler environments and attendance at school was lowest in the summer. So that became the time for the big vacation. Summer Slide Is Real As any teacher will tell you, the “summer slide” – the loss of academic knowledge and functioning that occurs over summer break – is real, especially in low-income communities. Some research has found that the loss can be as much as one month. The questions then are: is the slide a problem and if so, how do we fight it? Should We Worry? Our first response as educators and parents is…Yes! But let’s examine this more carefully. Sports have off-seasons. Enjoy the summer and fight the “Summer Slide.” We all sleep. Performers don’t go year-round. Rest is an important part of healthy growth since it is where we can recover and solidify our gains. While the summer slide leads to a loss of learning, the information is not permanently lost. It just shifts away from the most readily available part of the brain. It often takes only a week to regain what we have “lost” over the summer. The flip side is that losing our scholastic gains can be a problem. Students work very hard to learn, score and achieve. To watch all of that wither away as our students play video games and sleep until 3:30 pm is difficult and scary. pages.text: Wednesday, May 25, 2022 7 Thinking Outside The Classroom Summer vacation: How can we use it? By Paul Osborne There is a common misconception that summer vacation is a relic of the agrarian past when kids would be let out of school in the summer to help with the farming duties. While there is some truth to the notion that kids in rural communities took time off from school to help, this happened in the spring and fall when planting and harvesting occurred. Winter and summer were when many schools in agrarian societies met since that is when the kids had more free time. So where did the summer break come from? Escaping the heat. Before the school calendars were nationally synchronized, many schools were open yearround and students showed up whenever they could or chose to. The extreme heat of the East Coast summers caused many urban residents to escape to cooler environments and attendance at school was lowest in the summer. So that became the time for the big vacation. Summer Slide Is Real As any teacher will tell you, the “summer slide” – the loss of academic knowledge and functioning that occurs over summer break – is real, especially in low-income communities. Some research has found that the loss can be as much as one month. The questions then are: is the slide a problem and if so, how do we fight it? Should We Worry? Our first response as educators and parents is…Yes! But let’s examine this more carefully. Sports have off-seasons. Enjoy the summer and fight the “Summer Slide.” We all sleep. Performers don’t go year-round. Rest is an important part of healthy growth since it is where we can recover and solidify our gains. While the summer slide leads to a loss of learning, the information is not permanently lost. It just shifts away from the most readily available part of the brain. It often takes only a week to regain what we have “lost” over the summer. The flip side is that losing our scholastic gains can be a problem. Students work very hard to learn, score and achieve. To watch all of that wither away as our students play video games and sleep until 3:30 pm is difficult and scary. Plus, we have to wonder if our students would do even better if they gained instead of lost during the summer. How to Fight the Slide There are a myriad of ways to fight the summer slide, and there is no best way to do it. There is a consensus to keep their minds working. This can involve science-based camps, strategy games, summer school, yearround school, an hour of flashcards a day, etc… The point is not necessarily finding the optimal way to fight the slide, but finding any way to fight the slide and make sure it happens. pages.text: Wednesday, May 25, 2022 11 8th graders celebrate with traditional Boat Dance By Jay Russell After a two-year hiatus Piedmont Middle School was able to send its 8th grade graduates out on the Bay to enjoy the traditional year-end Boat Dance. The fun-filled evening took place on the Hornblower Empress from Event organizers Barbara Dickason (left), Michelle Heafey, and Jenny Osman Middle School administrators THE BEST CARE FOR YOUR BEST FRIEND Berkeley Marina. The kids were treated to casino games, a bountiful buffet of food, a photo booth, a DJ, and dancing. The weather was perfect for a tour of the Bay, including McCovey Cove, views of Alcatraz, and a trip under the Golden Gate Bridge. articles.text: The Piedmont Mountain Bike Team sent 11 riders to the Northern California Championships at Six Sigma Ranch in Clear Lake on Saturday May 21. It marked a return to the annual championship race for the first time in three years due to the global pandemic. The Norcal League includes 1500 high school riders in 85 teams. More than half of Piedmont;s riders qualified for the Championship meet, including Artun Duransoy (varsity), Heather Stoneman (JV girls), Andres Roberts, Kurt Wilson, Griffin Stein and Aleksi Valkonen (JV Boys), Schuyler Sawicki, Matteo Scanu, Max Rivera, and Mark Hsia (Sophomore boys), and Cary Ward (Freshmen boys). The Championship course was six miles on a windy single track with a lot of elevation changes, including a few water crossings In the Sophomore boys category, Schuyler Sawicki finished seventh out of 60 riders with a time of 1:04:02 in two laps. Matteo Scanu was two seconds back in 9th place. Schuyler and Matteo jointly won the team award for the greatest achievement in the season. Max Rivera finished 22nd and was named the team’s most improved rider for the season. Mark Hsia finished 29tth. “Congratulations to Schuyler and Matteo for finishing in the top 10 riders in D1 in Northern California in the Sophomore Boys category at the 2022 Championships,” said coach Sally Aldridge. “They both have worked very hard all season.” In the JV Boys category, Junior Andres Roberts was 14th out of 73 with a time of 1:38:23 over three laps. In Kurt Wilson’s final race as a senior, he finished 32nd after starting at the back of the field and passing 40 riders. Juniors Griffin Stein finished 40th and Aleksi Valkonen was 43rd In the Varsity boys field, Duransoy had to retire after two laps due to a knee injury. After a rest, he returned to the course in a valiant effort to finish. In JV Girls, junior Heather Stoneman was 50th out of 53 over two laps. Training for next season starts in the Fall. For more information go to www.piedmontmtb.com or email piedmontbiking@gmail. com. Schuyler Sawicki finished seventh out of 60 riders with a time of 1:04:02 in the two-lap Sophomore Boys category. Sophomore Matteo Scanu was ninth in 1:06:09. Andres Roberts was 14th of 73 in the JV Boys race with a time of 1:38:23 on three laps.

Guests will view some of the world’s greatest urban vistas, while experiencing learning about the art of Michelangelo, Bernini, and Carlo Maderno, among others. “The city of Rome boasts some of the more noteworthy destinations in the Western World. articles.text: The Legion of Honor in San Francisco is showing Guo Pei: Couture Fantasy now through September 5. The fashion exhibit features the extraordinary designs of Chinese couture designer Guo Pei, who is widely considered China’s first couturier. More than 80 works over the past two decades will be on display, many of them were shown on Beijing and Paris runways. Pei is known for her craftsmanship, embroidery, and unconventional dressmaking techniques. “As a creator and artist, there is no greater honor than to share my creativity with a wider audience,” the artist said. “I hope that, through the artistry of couture and universal language of art, that it will foster cross-cultural appreciation, connections, and ideas.” To obtain tickets visit: https:// legionofhonor.famsf.org/guo-pei. The Guo Pei: Couture Fantasy exhibit is now on view at the Legion of Honor in San Francisco.

articles.text: San Francisco Opera will present Don Giovanni beginning June 4 and running through July 2. The concerto was one of Schumann’s last works and has had difficulty making it as a standard work. It is dramatic and hot blooded from the outset - and then the patented Schumann tenderness is applied to offset the drama. It is a worthy piece despite some misgivings. articles.text: World-renowned are Stanford University’s technology expertise and her women’s sports teams. But across town, there’s a little miracle called West Bay Opera, which despite a postagestamp-sized auditorium to play in, brings off productions that are both presentable and downright moving. Cheers should ring out with WBO resuming performances after the two-year Covid padlock, now hitting its stride in its 66th season. Imagine a theater incapable of scene changes. Half the musicians are sitting in the wings like caged birds, barely able to see the baton of conductor Juan Luis Moscovich, who must also double as the company’s general director. In Tchaikovsky’s Queen of Spades, you have armies of performers, including some unpaid choruses, walk-ons, children, and a trio of Commedia dell’Arte dancer-singers who nearly stole the show in their cameo (at least, when not hopscotching over footlights). The performance on May 20 – the phoenix rising from the viral ashes. a fateful drama about gambling, gamboling, and the supernatural – came off powerfully at the heart of the matter, at least if you didn’t examine the edges too much. The cast sang in Russian. And if your vocabulary never went beyond “Tri karti” (3 cards) and “Ya vas lyublyu” (I love you), you had the projected text translations to help out. It has weaknesses common to the genre, like pieces stopping the drama dead in its tracks with irrelevant choral scenes – once proclaiming a sunny day, later judging it a stormy day. To their credit Verdi operas eliminated those fillers with choruses propelling the action or juicy subplots to replace fillers. But the racy central story, with assignations and secret rendezvous, is engrossing. A man, Hermann, caught between a love interest in Liza and an obsession for gambling at cards in scenes of the elegant Czarist aristocracy. He loves the gaming table more, literally forcing an old clairvoyant Countess to divulge future outcomes and enable him to make his fortune. In the end the ghost of the victimized Countess thwarts his greed with a flawed prediction. The turning up of the queen of spades in the casino leads to his merited end. WBO made the seven-scene opera work through dazzling architectural projections. The masterful touch was a lovers’ quarrel at the walls of the canal where, as if in a video, the image slowly shifts to the canal waters, showing the demise in a watery suicide – a great touch by projection designer Peter Compton. The heavyweight voices of Michael Boley (Hermann) and Rhoslyn Jones (Liza) rang through the hall and rafters with power and authority. They cautiously tended to the sharp side vocally to skirt tending flat. Jones’ surprising mobility added plausibility to the doomed pair. In the scene-stealing secondary role of the Countess, mezzo Laure de Marcellus proved to be the night’s best actress. In strong supporting low voices of nobles came Kiril Havezov (Tomsky) and Jonathan Beyer (Yelensky). Audience sympathies had to be with WBO, playing a 19th-century Russian opera at a time of great public antipathy toward Russia, a factor definitely cutting into attendance at the opener. But given the many months of contracted operatic preparation, WBO was in a position to substitute Otello, Mme. Butterfly or Porgy and Bess. Stage Director Ragnar Conde did some of his best work staging the song-and-dance trio of Commedia dell’arte performers Sarah Benzinger, Maria Kaganskaya and Kiril Havezov in the Masked Ball scene. For the audience, Vaccination ID was required and masks strongly recommended. articles.text: Bouquets to Art, the de Young Museum’s premiere fundraiser and annual display of artwork-inspired floral installations, will begin on June 7. Bouquets to Art, now in its 38th year, is back to full-capacity following a virtual event in 2020 and a hybrid, limited-capacity event last year. For one week, more than 100 experienced floral designers will converge at the de Young to showcase arrangements inspired by the museum’s vast array of paintings, sculptures, and architecture. Bouquets to Art is one of the Fine Arts Museum of San Francisco’s most popular and well-attended events every year. The event is presented by the volunteer members of the fine arts museums - and draws nearly 800,000 visitors a year, with net proceeds of more than $7 million. Funds from the event help underwrite special exhibitions, conservation projects, and educational programming. Bouquets to Art in a photo from 2015 Photo by Thomas Henthorne Guests will be greeted with a large-scale aerial artwork piece by Bay Area artist Windy Chien. Entitled The Three Dragons, the hand-knotted artwork hangs in the museum’s Wilsey Court. Those who visit during the week of Bouquets to Art will have a chance to view Hung Liu’s large piece Resident Alien, first exhibited at the Capp Street Project in 1988 and exhibited by the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco last year. The painting, arguably Liu’s most famous, depicts her own “Green Card” on a larger-than-life scale. It is now in the collection of the San Jose Museum of Art. “Hung Liu is uniquely positioned to tell the stories of immigrants to the United States. In 2020, she celebrated the milestone of having lived an equal number of years in China and the United States. As one of the foremost painters in the United States, Liu is a testament to the fact that our brightest citizens are often born under foreign skies,” said Janna Keegan, Assistant Curator of Contemporary Art and Programming at the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco. Bouquets to Art is a weeklong event that begins on Monday evening, June 6, with an opening-night reception. Between June 7 and June 12, a series of book launches, speaker events, and raffles will take place. For a full list of programming, visit https://www.famsf.org/pressroom/bouquets-art. Tickets sold out weeks prior to the event in 2021 - reserve yours now by visiting https://deyoung. famsf.org/bouquets-to-art.

articles.text: The film Crazy Heart, released in 2010 and published in The Post the same year, is one of those rare films that examines a character with insight and, in its own way, affection. That isn’t to say that country western singer Bad Blake (Jeff Bridges) is by any stretch attractive. Charming to be sure, in a dissipated, chain-smoking, alcoholic, resolutely self-destructive way. After decades on the road, he’s beyond the nadir of his career as a performer and song writer, now solidly middle-aged, broke and playing bowling alleys in adjunct lounges named “The Spare Room,” or small, smoky bars frequented by those who remember when and still resonate to lyrics like, “I use to be somebody, but now I’m somebody else.” His nights are spent in seedy motels, sometimes in the company of a woman who looks at Blake and sees only a memory, that once deeply talented musician/singer and not the staggering wreck of a man who rushes off the stage and vomits in a back alley. Clearly that sounds grim, but it’s not. Bridges’ portrayal of Blake is compelling – a fascinating study of a man circling the drain who can still muster the will to live, singing music that remains embedded in his heart. Maggie Gyllenhaal portrays Jean Craddock, a young journalist in Santa Fe, who shows up at one of Blake’s gigs asking for an interview for the local paper. She’s lovely, a single mom, and attracted to Blake for reasons that are never really clear. She acknowledges that she isn’t looking for another man to break her heart, or a man whose life is dominated by alcohol (“It’s like living with a rattlesnake”). articles.text: Initially the title Paper Towns seems enigmatic, puzzling. Paper towns, apparently, are fake destinations, used by cartographers as a way of copyrighting their work. It’s a metaphor soon explained. The film is a coming-of-age story set in Orlando, Florida, involving seniors in high school on the cusp of graduating. At the movie’s center is Quentin Jacobsen (Nat Wolff), a quintessential nerd, and his two best friends, Ben (Austin Abrams) and Radar (Justice Smith). In the opening set up, Q explains in voice over that from the first day that he saw Margo Roth Spiegelman (Cara Delevingne), moving in across the street, he has been in love with her (they were both 10). Even during high school, when Margo becomes popular and Q, Ben and Radar are on the fringe of the school’s social hierarchy, he’s still crazy about her. They pass each other in the halls like strangers and it breaks his heart. Late one night Margo appears at his window. She talks him into taking his family car and driving her to the houses of some kids. The first is Margo’s best friend, with whom her boyfriend has been cheating. Margo is wild and reckless. Q is conservative and has had his nose to the academic grindstone for the last four years. He’s going to Duke U. and wants to be a doctor. Take his mom’s van? No way. But then this is Margo Roth Spiegelman, the girl of his dreams, excessively cool and Halston Sage and Nat Wolff in a scene from Paper Towns. alluring and mysterious. On second thought. articles.text: Joey Cramer stars in Flight of the Navigator. The Flight of the Navigator, released in 1986 by Disney, will definitely appeal to a new generation of tweens and teens. Using what was then groundbreaking CGI, this time-travel adventure stars Joey Cramer portraying a 12-year-old boy named David Freeman. The setting is Ft. Lauderdale, the year is 1978, the day is July 4, and David is walking through the woods on his way to pick up his 8-year-old brother, Jeff (Matt Adler). Lost in thought, not watching where he is going, David tumbles into a ravine and is knocked unconscious. When he comes to, he runs home and finds that strangers are living in his house. When he is finally reunited with his parents, Helen and Bill (Veronica Cartwright and Cliff DeYoung), to his surprise he finds them and brother Jeff now eight years older. We learn that David was abducted by aliens, placed on a spaceship, and transported to the distant planet Phaelon, some 560 light years away. Exceeding the speed of light, time is distorted and while David remains the same age, eight years pass by on earth while only some two hours have gone by for David. The spaceship, we learn, is commanded by a robotic computer named Max (Paul Reubens), and during the journey David is studied by the aliens. When returning David to the ravine, the ship crashes and is captured by NASA. A group of scientists, headed by Dr. Louis Faraday (Howard Hesseman), convince David to come to NASA, where they examine him. They discover that his brain is filled with star charts and techie information that far exceeds anything known to researchers on earth, thus they treat him like a research subject. Realizing that the manipulative Faraday is actually holding David and Max captive, the two manage to escape and using telepathy signal the ship. Max tells David that the navigational charts he has in his head are needed if Max and crew are ever to return to Phaelon. For David it proves to be quite an adventure. And, of course, as narratives of this ilk go, David does wonder if his experience was only a dream. He soon discovers that nothing has changed. Time has passed – yet it hasn’t. It’s still the 4th of July and of course there are fireworks launched to celebrate that much-anticipated day. Kids will enjoy what proves to be a compelling, and underrated sci-fi tale filled with twists and turns. Flight of the Navigator. Directed by Randall Kleiser. articles.text: Will Adams Talking with Group A walking tour led by Will Adams drew a big crowd on May 18 for Walking on Wednesdays. Pictured are: Priscilla Wanerus, Jo Normington with K-9 best friend Penny Lane, Alicia Rivera, Lois Price, Edith Lee, Stella Houston, Noemi Alvarado, Siow Fang Tan, Brenda Ferrero, Judy Wang, Dave DeRoche, Helen Dong, Swee Ling Chen, Phil Witte, Tami DeSellier, Jim Kuo, Albert Chen, Kat Lang, Harriette Louie, Sherry Jacobs, Eric Behrens, Adrienne Hamlin, Joyce Hicks, Pat Sheehan, Pat Keller, Dena Belinkoff, Melba Yee, Laura Goldman, Aaron Katzel, Sarah Johnson, Ellen Manolis, Nadine Guffanti, Martin Levy, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Cheryl Stanton, Christine Calliste, Nancy DeRoche, John Lenahan, Elizabeth Richter, Mike Henn with K-9 best friend Roger, Quincy Dong, and Dick Carter. The group was pleased to welcome first time walkers Christina Miller, Kirk Miller, Corky Roberts, Molly Roberts, Raymond Ritter, and others. John Malick, a local architect and friend of Will, was there to join in the fun too. The Piedmont Recreation Depar tment’s Walking on Wednesdays group came close to needing a parade permit last Wednesday, May 18. There were a total of 55 walkers and three K-9 best friends who met at the Exedra Plaza on a beautiful morning. However, they didn’t attend just for the weather. Piedmont planner, urban designer, and architect Will Adams was there to lead a special walking tour of historical Piedmont buildings designed by famed architect Albert Farr. Nancy and Dave DeRoche invited everyone to their home the following Wednesdasy for a follow up to the tour with Will. Nancy and Dave reported that Albert Farr lived in their house on Oakland Avenue for 25 years in the early 20th Century. Will Adams provided an introduction to and overview of Albert L. Farr. He was an American architect, who during the first decades of Piedmont’s development, designed many homes and some of Piedmont’s most prominent buildings, including the City Hall, Piedmont Community Church and the Piedmont Community Center. Farr was born in Omaha, Nebraska, but grew up in Yokohama, Japan. The Farr family returned to the United States in 1891, and settled in the San Francisco Bay Area. Farr lived at various times in San Francisco, Berkeley, Oakland, and Piedmont where he died in 1945 at age 76. Farr earned his architecture license in 1901, one of the first in California, and was designing grand mansions for his clients while still in his 20s. His clients were primarily in the San Francisco in the neighborhoods of Russian Hill, Pacific Heights, Seacliff, and St. Francis Wood. Farr also designed prominent estate homes and commercial and public buildings in Belvedere, Woodside, and Piedmont and had a strong interest in planning and urban design. He the Exedra, as well as the layout of “downtown” Piedmont. Will asked the walkers to evaluate the urban design of the town center and how well connected the various key buildings are. Will talked about Farr’s architectural training and how architects will study and apply different styles to their work. Farr’s use of the Spanish Revival styles in the Piedmont public buildings has defined to a large degree the character of Piedmont. Will took the group to City Hall to illustrate both the symmetrical (more formal) and asymmetrical (less formal) design approaches Farr employed on his different buildings. Will noted the “outdoor room” to the right of the City Hall’s entrance now with replica concrete benches that provide a well-used informal meeting place. Will said there is a relief hidden behind climbing vines on the front of the City Hall that he wished was visible. Will then led the group through Piedmont Park, past the Farr-designed Community Hall on Highland Avenue to Wildwood Avenue and an historic mansion at the corner of Sheridan. The estate was just sold. Behind its wrought iron gate, Will talked about Farr’s classical training that allowed him to add architectural details, like interesting rain downspouts, to enhance the house’s beautiful design. He also noted how Farr mitigated what an Asian audience would consider the negative feng shui of a straight-on axial street at the house’s front gate with a lovely water fountain in front of the house’s entrance. Next was a walk to the foot of Lincoln Avenue to see how Farr had integrated the features of different European architectural styles in a home. Visible through the front door was an outdoor water fountain. It was then on to a home on Mountain Avenue that Will’s architect friend, John Malick, had remodeled. John, who was on the tour, shared some ideas architects use to satisfy the desires and budgets of clients. The final stop was the Piedmont Community Church. The group went up its front steps to the church’s lovely courtyard with roses in full bloom. Will noted that it was Mission Revival style, with its simplified execution that limited the construction expense, while keeping its design compatible with other important buildings in Piedmont’s center. In the church’s sanctuary Will pointed out the impressive ceiling trellises and confessed he had once copied this Farr design concept for one of his projects. The slope from the back of the church to its front was also noted, and the better visibility of the service that it provides worshipers was appreciated. At the conclusion of the tour, the group expressed their appreciation for Will and the informative tour he led. They were also pleased that they would have another opportunity to talk with Will next Wednesday when they all visit the DeRoches. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation is required at https:// tinyurl.com/3ethkehu. articles.text: As an investor, you can easily feel frustrated to see short-term drops in your investment statements. But while you cannot control the market, you may find it helpful to review the factors you can control. Many forces affect the financial markets, including geopolitical events, corporate profits and interest rate movements – forces beyond the control of most individual investors. In any case, it’s important to focus on the things you can control, such as these: • Your ability to define your goals – One area in which you have total control is your ability to define your goals. Like most people, you probably have short-term goals – such as saving for a new car or a dream vacation – and long-term ones, such as a comfortable retirement. articles.text: Albert Farr designed the elegant Mediterranean home at 395 Hampton Road in Piedmont in 1927 in his iconic style with a grand arched entry surrounded by quoins and a cartouche and finials above. Tall windows, a Spanish tile roof, shutters and a symmetrical façade complete his design. The house sits behind a circular driveway which retains the original light poles. New lights at the entry match the original lights. Marble steps lead to metal double doors with original nailhead detail and windows with spindles. In the foyer, architect Farr placed French doors leading to the living room, game room, dining room, and rear terrace and gardens for excellent flow from room to room. To the left, double doors open to the impressive 30-foot living room filled with southern light from tall windows. The ceilings throughout the house are high and were designed to accommodate the original owner’s large artwork and furniture. Wood beams enrich the living room, dining room and library ceilings. Beyond, the sunroom provides an intimate, well-lit room to relax. Farr reportedly returned two years after the house was built to convert the former terrace to a sunroom with the resulting room above in the master suite. The original library, now used as a game room, provides a casual spot for gathering with family and friends by the fireplace. Two sets of tall French doors open to the rear garden and terrace. The mirrored bar off the foyer opens to the rear terrace, and conveniently provides a sink, refrigerator, and dishwasher for entertaining indoors and out. The spacious dining room across the entry foyer continues Farr’s high ceiling design. More tall windows bring in light and provide garden views for diners. The high ceilings extend to the handsome, modern kitchen beyond with a large center island, range, second sink and seating for six. The freezer and refrigerators are faced to match the cabinets. Dishwashers, a steam oven with warming drawer and a roomy pantry with a ladder to reach the top shelves add to the conveniences of this up-to-date kitchen. The banquette provides more eat-in dining, and the adjacent sunny patio offers outdoor dining. The kitchen area extends to a coffee bar beyond, laundry room, former maid’s room, and a full bath. The reconfigured mud room provides convenient access to the driveway, parking pad and garages. From the foyer, the graceful, curving stairway with slender wrought-iron balustrade leads to five generously-sized bedrooms with ensuite baths and several bonus rooms on the second floor. The stained-glass skylight above this circular staircase dates to the original 1927 design. The grand master suite has a gas fireplace to warm the room, sunny windows that overlook the front garden, and an adjacent sunroom offering views of the redwood trees. Albert Farr was a well-respected architect in the Bay Area and practiced from 1905 to 1937. He has been called one of the most artistic architects on the West Coast. He is known for his Period Revival designs of large homes with monumental entries and generous public rooms with high ceilings, often trimmed with elegant woodwork. Farr designed more than 40 homes in Piedmont, and six Farr-designed houses have been on Decorator Showcase tours. Farr’s brother, Harry St. Sure Farr, was on the Piedmont Board of Trustees, and early in his career he designed the Bonita Avenue School in 1909, the predecessor of Havens School, Piedmont’s City Hall (1910), and the Oakland Avenue Bridge (1910). The city is able to use 140 units to meet its Regional Housing Needs Allocation (RHNA) because it has a track record of producing up to 17 ADUs a year over the last three years, explained Piedmont Senior Planner Pierce Macdonald-Powell. “The 140 new ADUs are based on the average building permit activity from the last three years [17.5 ADUs], extrapolated out 8 years [17.5 x 8 years = 140 ADUs.],” she said. “We may see more ADUs constructed in the future, but State HCD limits each city to the prior averaged rate of construction.” Last chance for public input The City Council meeting will be a last-chance opportunity to provide public comment on the draft housing element before it heads to HCD for review. However, it will not be the last time for public comment on the 6th housing element before it is officially adopted in Spring 2023. Once Piedmont receives review findings from HCD, it can then revise the housing element to comply with the statute and adopt it, or adopt the draft without revising it. Assembly Bill 215, approved by Gov. Gavin Newsom in September 2021, requires that prior to submittal of the first draft to the HCD, all local governments must make the draft available for public comment for at least 30 days, and if any comments were received, take at least 10 business days to consider and incorporate public comments in the draft. Since the publication of the draft housing element, the city has discussed the document during its most recent public Park Commission, Planning Commission, and Recreation Commission meetings, as well as during Housing Advisory Committee Meetings.
